category.name: Image & Video Verification
category.description: Establishing whether a photograph or video is what it claims to be: where it came from, when it first appeared, whether it has been altered, and whether it has been recycled from an earlier event. This is the discipline that separates verified reporting from amplified rumour.

tools.name: ExifTool
tools.summary: The reference tool for reading and writing metadata in images, video, audio and documents.
tools.description:
ExifTool, by Phil Harvey, reads essentially every metadata format in existence: EXIF, IPTC, XMP, GPS tags, maker notes specific to individual camera models, and the container metadata in video and document formats. It is a command-line tool and it is the standard against which other metadata readers are measured.

In verification it is the first thing you run on any file you actually hold. Capture timestamp, camera make and model, lens, GPS coordinates, editing software, and the sequence of modification dates are all potential leads, and the maker-note fields sometimes include serial numbers and settings that are highly distinctive.

The overriding limit: almost every social media platform strips metadata on upload. A file downloaded from Twitter, Facebook, Instagram or WhatsApp will usually have nothing. Metadata is also trivially forgeable — ExifTool itself writes metadata as readily as it reads it. Present metadata is a lead requiring corroboration; absent metadata means nothing at all; and metadata that seems too helpful deserves more suspicion, not less.
tools.costNotes: Free and open source, released under the Perl Artistic and GPL licences. No account, no limits.
tools.legalNotes: Runs entirely locally on files you already possess, which makes it the safest option in this category: nothing is uploaded, no third party learns what you are examining, and no subject is notified. That is a decisive advantage over browser-based metadata viewers when the material is sensitive. Extracted GPS coordinates are personal data about whoever took the image and should be handled accordingly.
tools.reliabilityNotes: The most complete and accurate metadata implementation available; it reports what is in the file, correctly, including fields other tools miss. Reliability of the metadata itself is an entirely separate question — timestamps depend on a correctly set camera clock, GPS depends on a fix that may have been poor, and every field can be fabricated. ExifTool is trustworthy; EXIF is not.
tools.confidenceNotes: Long-established reference implementation, continuously maintained for over two decades. Not fetched during this review.

tools.name: Jeffrey's Image Metadata Viewer
tools.summary: Browser-based EXIF viewer for a quick metadata read without installing anything.
tools.description:
Jeffrey Friedl's metadata viewer accepts an uploaded image or a URL and displays its EXIF, IPTC and XMP metadata in a readable layout, plotting any GPS coordinates on a map.

It exists in this catalogue as the convenient option, not the correct one. When you need a fast look at a non-sensitive image and cannot run ExifTool, it does the job well and has done for many years.

The caveat is the whole point of the entry: using it means uploading your evidence to a third-party server, or asking that server to fetch a URL on your behalf. For any material that is confidential, that identifies a source, or that belongs to a live investigation, that is an unacceptable disclosure. Use ExifTool locally instead. The convenience is not worth the exposure.
tools.legalNotes: Uploading an image transfers it to a third party. If the image contains personal data, that transfer is itself a processing act you are responsible for, and if it identifies a source it may compromise them. Fetching by URL causes the service to request the URL, which appears in the host's logs — so it can disclose to a target that their content is being examined. Prefer local analysis for anything sensitive.
tools.reliabilityNotes: Accurate and long-standing for the mainstream metadata fields, though less exhaustive than ExifTool on obscure maker notes. Same caveat as all metadata work: what it shows is what the file claims, which may be wrong or forged. Availability of long-running hobby services is never guaranteed.
tools.confidenceNotes: A long-established tool, but it is an individually maintained service on a plain HTTP endpoint and its current availability was not verified during this review. Confirm it loads before including it in a workflow, and prefer ExifTool regardless.

tools.name: TinEye
tools.summary: Reverse image search that finds exact and modified copies of an image, sortable by oldest first.
tools.description:
TinEye indexes images and matches on the image itself rather than on surrounding text. Given a picture it returns pages where that image, or a cropped, resized, recoloured or lightly edited version of it, appears.

One feature makes it disproportionately valuable for verification: results can be sorted by oldest. That directly answers the central question about a supposedly new image — has this appeared before? Finding the same photograph on a blog from four years ago settles a recycled-image claim in seconds, and it does so with a citable URL and date.

TinEye is deliberately literal. It does not find visually similar but different scenes, which makes it precise and gives it a low false-positive rate, but it also means it will not find a different photograph of the same location. Its index is also smaller than Google's, and heavily recompressed or substantially cropped images often fail to match. A null result is weak evidence: always run the same image through at least two other reverse-image engines before concluding it is new.
tools.costNotes: Web search is free without an account. A paid API is sold in credit bundles and subscription tiers for programmatic and commercial use. Current prices were not verified in this review.
tools.legalNotes: Uploading an image sends it to TinEye. For sensitive material — an image from a source, or a photograph of a private individual — consider whether that disclosure is acceptable before searching. Search by URL causes a fetch of that URL. Results are pointers to third-party pages whose own copyright and use terms apply.
tools.reliabilityNotes: High precision: a TinEye match is almost always a genuine match, which is why it is trusted for the 'has this appeared before' question. Recall is the weakness — a smaller index than Google's and poorer performance on heavily edited or recompressed images mean many true earlier appearances are missed. The oldest-result date is the date TinEye crawled or the page reports, not a forensic determination of first publication.
tools.confidenceNotes: Long-established commercial service with a stable free web search. Not fetched during this review; API pricing unverified.

tools.name: Google Lens
tools.summary: Google's visual search — strong at recognising places, objects, text and visually similar scenes.
tools.description:
Google Lens performs visual search over Google's index. Unlike TinEye it is semantic rather than literal: it recognises what is in an image and finds related content, which means it can identify a landmark, read and translate text in a sign, name a product or plant, and surface visually similar scenes that are not copies.

For geolocation this is often the fastest first move. Feeding it a photograph of an unfamiliar building or streetscape sometimes returns the location outright, and even when it does not, its guesses about architectural style or region narrow the search. Its text recognition on signage, in scripts you cannot read, is a genuine capability that opens investigations.

The corresponding danger is that semantic matching is confident and frequently wrong. Lens will assert a plausible-looking location for a generic scene with no indication of uncertainty. It is a hypothesis generator. Every suggestion must be confirmed by matching identifiable features against independent imagery before it counts as anything.
tools.costNotes: Free to use through Google Search, the Chrome browser and the Google mobile apps. No dedicated public API for this catalogue's purposes.
tools.legalNotes: Images uploaded are processed by Google and become part of your interaction with a commercial platform that logs it against your account or session. For sensitive material, and particularly for images of identifiable private individuals, weigh that disclosure. Note that Google restricts face matching in Lens results — do not attempt to work around that, and this platform will not assist with it.
tools.reliabilityNotes: Excellent at landmarks, text, products and distinctive scenes; unreliable and confidently wrong on generic scenes such as ordinary streets, fields and interiors. It presents guesses without calibrated uncertainty. Treat every result as a lead. Results also vary by account, language and region, so two analysts can get different answers for the same image — record what you saw and when.
tools.confidenceNotes: Widely used, current Google product. Not fetched during this review; the entry point and interface change frequently as Google reorganises visual search.

tools.name: Yandex Images
tools.summary: Reverse image search with unusually strong performance on faces, people and Eastern European content.
tools.description:
Yandex's reverse image search has a long-standing reputation among OSINT practitioners for finding matches that Google and TinEye miss, particularly for photographs of people, and for content originating in Russia, Ukraine and the wider region. Its similarity matching is aggressive, returning visually related images rather than only copies.

That aggressiveness is genuinely useful for geolocation — it will surface other photographs of the same building or street taken from different angles, which is exactly what you need to confirm a location.

Two cautions, both serious. First, its strength on faces means using it to find other pictures of a person edges toward face-matching, which this platform does not do and which carries the biometric-data exposure described in the PimEyes entry — using a general search engine does not change the legal character of what you are doing. Second, Yandex is a Russian-jurisdiction service: assume your queries are logged and potentially accessible to Russian state authorities. For any investigation touching Russian interests, or involving a source who would be endangered by that, this is a serious operational-security decision and often the correct answer is not to use it.
tools.costNotes: Free to use without an account.
tools.legalNotes: The operator is subject to Russian law, including data-localisation and state-access requirements. Assume queries and uploaded images are retained and may be accessible to state authorities. Uploading an image of an identifiable person to a face-capable similarity engine in order to find that person raises the same GDPR Article 9 biometric issues as a dedicated face-search service, regardless of the tool's general-purpose framing. Do not use it against private individuals, and think hard before using it at all in a matter where Russian state interest is plausible.
tools.reliabilityNotes: Real and frequently decisive extra recall, especially regionally, but a much higher false-positive rate than TinEye because it returns similarity rather than identity. Results are inconsistent between sessions and regions. Every match must be confirmed by identifiable shared detail, not by an impression that two images look alike.
tools.confidenceNotes: Long-established and widely used. Not fetched during this review; accessibility from some networks and jurisdictions varies.

tools.name: InVID-WeVerify Verification Plugin
tools.summary: Browser extension bundling video keyframe extraction, multi-engine reverse search, metadata and forensic filters.
tools.description:
The InVID-WeVerify plugin — distributed through browser extension stores as the 'Fake news debunker by InVID, WeVerify & vera.ai' — is the closest thing the verification community has to a standard toolkit. It emerged from EU-funded research projects and remains actively developed.

Its most valuable function is keyframe extraction. Reverse image search works on stills, not video, so verifying a video means pulling representative frames and searching each one. The plugin does that automatically from a URL or file and then fires each keyframe at several reverse-image engines in one action. It also reads video and image metadata, queries platform APIs for upload timestamps, applies forensic filters, and provides magnification and analysis tools.

Limits: it orchestrates other services rather than replacing them, so it inherits all their limitations, and individual modules break when the platforms they query change. Its forensic filters, like all such filters, indicate anomalies worth investigating and do not determine that an image was manipulated. Install it only from an official browser extension store.
tools.costNotes: Free. Distributed through the Chrome Web Store and equivalent Edge and Opera add-on stores. Developed under EU-funded research projects; no account is required for core functions, though some modules may require one.
tools.legalNotes: Operates in your browser but sends content to third-party services when you invoke reverse search or platform lookups — the same disclosure considerations as those services individually. As a browser extension it necessarily has access to page content, so install only from an official store and only in a browser profile you are comfortable giving it. Downloading video from a platform may breach that platform's terms of service.
tools.reliabilityNotes: The keyframe and reverse-search workflow is dependable and saves substantial time. Individual modules degrade without warning as upstream platforms change their APIs, so a module returning nothing may be broken rather than reporting a true negative — check a known-good example before trusting a null result. Forensic filters are indicative only and are routinely over-read as proof of manipulation.
tools.confidenceNotes: Confirmed during this review as current and actively developed, with a version shipped in July 2025 and continuing commits into April 2026, and available through official browser extension stores. The canonical project page URL given here should be preferred for reference, but install from the extension store rather than any third-party download.

tools.name: Forensically
tools.summary: Browser-based image forensics suite — error level analysis, clone detection, noise analysis, magnifier — running entirely client-side.
tools.description:
Forensically, by Jonas Wagner, provides a set of image-analysis filters in the browser: error level analysis, clone detection, noise analysis, level sweep, luminance gradient, principal component analysis and a strong magnifier.

It has one significant operational advantage over most online forensic tools: the analysis runs client-side in your browser, so the image is not uploaded to a server. For sensitive material that is a meaningful difference, though you should verify current behaviour yourself rather than take it on trust.

The essential caveat applies to the entire class of tools and cannot be repeated too often. Error level analysis and its relatives do not detect manipulation. They visualise compression, noise and resampling artefacts, which are affected by editing but are also affected by resizing, re-saving, screenshotting, platform processing and the camera's own pipeline. An image passed through a social platform will show anomalies that mean nothing. ELA has produced a long history of confident, public, wrong accusations of forgery. Use these filters to find regions worth examining, then prove manipulation by other means — provenance, an earlier version, an internal inconsistency in the scene — or do not claim it.
tools.costNotes: Free to use in a browser with no account.
tools.legalNotes: Client-side processing means the image is not transmitted to the operator, which makes it comparatively safe for confidential material — but confirm that behaviour in your own browser's network tools before relying on it for something genuinely sensitive.
tools.reliabilityNotes: The filters are correctly implemented; the reliability problem is interpretive and severe. ELA output is routinely misread as proof of editing by people who do not understand that recompression produces identical artefacts. Clone detection produces false positives on repetitive natural textures. Nothing from this tool alone can establish that an image was manipulated. Rated 3 for the interpretation hazard, not for any defect in the software.
tools.confidenceNotes: Long-established, widely referenced free tool. Not fetched during this review.

tools.name: FotoForensics
tools.summary: Long-running image forensics service offering ELA, metadata, JPEG analysis and a public analysis archive.
tools.description:
FotoForensics, run by Neal Krawetz, is the best-known public image-forensics service. It provides error level analysis, metadata extraction, JPEG quantisation-table analysis and other views, alongside extensive tutorial material about how to read them and — unusually and to its credit — about how they are commonly misread.

The JPEG analysis is the underrated part. Quantisation tables and encoder fingerprints can indicate what software last wrote a file, which is a genuinely useful provenance signal: an image claimed to come straight from a phone that carries the signature of a desktop editor is worth explaining.

The critical operational fact: uploads to the free public service are retained and may be publicly accessible. Analysts have exposed confidential material this way. Do not upload anything sensitive, anything from a source, or anything belonging to a live investigation. The same interpretive caution as Forensically applies to all its ELA output — the site's own documentation says so, and analysts ignore it anyway.
tools.costNotes: A free public tier is available with no account, subject to retention and visibility conditions described on the site. Paid or private services have been offered separately for practitioners who need confidentiality. Current terms were not verified in this review.
tools.legalNotes: Uploads to the free service are retained by the operator and may be publicly visible in its archive. This is stated by the service and is regularly overlooked. Never upload confidential material, source-provided material, images of identifiable private individuals in a sensitive context, or anything under embargo. Use a local tool for those.
tools.reliabilityNotes: Well-implemented analyses backed by unusually good explanatory documentation. The JPEG and metadata analyses are solid provenance evidence. ELA carries the same severe misinterpretation risk described elsewhere in this category, and the service's own guidance is explicit that ELA does not prove manipulation. Rated 3 for interpretation hazard and upload exposure rather than software quality.
tools.confidenceNotes: Long-established service, stable for many years. Not fetched during this review; current retention and privacy terms should be read on the site before any upload.

tools.name: yt-dlp
tools.summary: Command-line downloader that preserves video from many platforms along with its metadata, subtitles and comments.
tools.description:
yt-dlp is an actively maintained fork of youtube-dl that downloads video and audio from a very large number of sites. For verification work its value is preservation and metadata rather than viewing.

Content central to an investigation gets deleted, and it gets deleted precisely when it becomes important. Capturing the highest-quality original — not a screen recording, not a re-upload — at the moment you find it is basic evidential hygiene, and yt-dlp can additionally save the upload timestamp, description, channel details, subtitles, thumbnails and comment threads as structured JSON alongside the media. Comments are frequently where a video's real context surfaces.

Working from the original file rather than a re-encode also matters technically: re-encoding destroys the compression characteristics that any subsequent forensic analysis would rely on.

Limits: extractors break constantly as platforms change, so it needs frequent updating. It cannot reach private, deleted or authentication-walled content, and it should not be used to try.
tools.costNotes: Free and open source, released into the public domain under the Unlicense. No account or key.
tools.legalNotes: Downloading from most major platforms is contrary to their terms of service, and this catalogue takes terms of service seriously. In several jurisdictions there is a recognised exception or defence for journalistic and archival purposes, but that is jurisdiction-specific and not universal, and the terms are breached regardless. Never use it to access content behind authentication or access controls you are not entitled to use — circumventing an access control is the line where terms-of-service breach becomes a computer-misuse offence. Downloaded material may contain personal data and copyright-protected work; possessing it for verification is different from republishing it.
tools.reliabilityNotes: Dependable and actively maintained, with a large contributor base. Individual site extractors break routinely when platforms change, so an outdated installation fails in ways that look like the content being unavailable. Update before concluding something cannot be retrieved. Reported metadata comes from the platform and inherits the platform's own inaccuracies, notably time zone handling on upload timestamps.
tools.confidenceNotes: Actively maintained, very widely used project. Repository not fetched during this review; extractor coverage changes with every release.
